The literature dates it to between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries, between the gopuz and the bağlama; it replaced the ozan gopuz in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries and was itself replaced by the saz in the fifteenth and sixteenth. In Caucasian, Iranian, Anatolian and Sufi traditions, dervishes and ashughs used instruments of the same name. In the early sixteenth century it was played in the Safavid army to raise morale. A nineteenth-century example has three courses and twenty-two frets. The Georgian chonguri appeared around the seventeenth century, and modern instruments add metal frets and pickups. Some versions survive among the peoples of the Caucasus and among the Turkmens of Iraq.
柯古爾是一種具有獨特魅力的中東弦樂器，音色溫潤而富有穿透力。其音質介於明亮與暗沉: The çöğür is a Middle Eastern string instrument with a character of its own, its timbre warm and carrying. Its sound sits between bright and dark, with a warm amber tint, and is highly expressive. The range is wide, covering high and low, the bass full and deep and the treble clear and transparent. The çöğür resonates through the cavity inside the body, so the sound rings and carries well. Against the oud its timbre has more penetration and force; against the violin it seems softer and plainer. Its plucked sound has a folk character and can carry many layers of feeling, which makes it an indispensable melodic instrument in Middle Eastern traditional music.

The çöğür is a plucked instrument popular in Azerbaijan and Georgia, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.321. The common construction has four nylon strings; the Georgian variant, the chonguri, is related to the panduri, with a larger body, traditionally fretless, and modern recording and stage instruments may add metal frets, tuning pegs and pickups. The Caucasian chungur comes in arrangements of four single strings, four double courses or seven strings. Historically, dervishes and ashughs in the Sufi tradition used instruments of this kind, and the Safavid army used it to raise morale; today it appears in ethno-jazz and similar performances.
柯古爾為弦鳴樂器，常見發聲體為尼龍弦，喬治亞傳統版本亦用腸弦。19世紀阿塞拜疆藏: The çöğür is a chordophone whose usual sounding body is nylon strings, and the traditional Georgian version also uses gut. The body of a nineteenth-century Azerbaijani example is made of mulberry, with a soundboard about four millimetres thick, the neck and head of nut wood and the tuning pegs of pear. Georgian instruments also favour thoroughly dried mulberry, and modern stage instruments add metal frets, tuning pegs and pickups. The Caucasian body may be carved from a single block or built into a circle from wooden ribs, and the frets are bound with thread or inlaid in metal. The materials of the other parts are not recorded.
柯古爾為撥弦樂器，常見於阿塞拜疆與喬治亞。歷史場合中，它曾用於蘇菲傳統、達爾維什: The çöğür is a plucked instrument, common in Azerbaijan and Georgia. Historically it was used in the Sufi tradition and played by dervishes and ashughs, and it raised morale in the army of the Safavid dynasty. The modern Georgian instrument appears in the studio and on stage, and it has entered ethno-jazz and genres drawn from traditional folk song, often sharing the stage with bass, acoustic guitar, electric guitar and percussion, and sometimes with digital synthesisers.
